To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the relationship between inequality and growth in a developing country is ambiguous.

(i) the effects of inequality on aggregate production and the incidence of unemployment are sensitive to the distribution of assets in an economy, (ii) in economies with large aggregate endowments, inequality has a negative effect on aggregate production and increases the incidence of unemployment, and (iii) in economies with small aggregate endowments inequality has a positive effect on aggregate production but increases the incidence of undernutrition and unemployment.
(a) the effects of inequality on growth are not monotonic and (b) the relationship between inequality and growth depends on the nature of inequality.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following question: What are the implications for economic policy if it is recognized that a person's "productive capacity" is an increasing (and not a decreasing) function of the quantity of food that he consumes?
the following issues: (i) How does the relationship between income inequality and poverty change when we account for the effects of inequality on growth and the determinants of inequality?

the following issues: (i) the role of the state in the economy, in particular the extent to which the state should intervene and regulate the private economy; (ii) the nature of the relationship between economic growth and poverty, and the role of the private sector in promoting growth; (iii) the role of foreign trade and foreign investment in economic growth; and (iv) the role of agriculture in economic development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is not sufficient to support a causal link between unemployment and health.
the evidence is not strong enough to support the view that the level of nutrition is a major determinant of economic growth.
there is no clear evidence of a direct link between inequality and economic growth.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inequality in the society is a cause of malnutrition and unemployment.
the paper provides a theoretical framework for analyzing the impact of inequality on the economy and on the incidence of undernutrition and unemployment.
the economic and social costs of malnutrition in developing countries are high and the benefits from investments in the nutrition sector are high.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to reduce inequality, the focus of policy should be on the poor, and that the rich do not need to be targeted in order to reduce the Gini coefficient.
inequality in the US has been increasing for decades.
inequality in the distribution of assets is a major cause of unemployment, malnutrition and other social evils.
